common_name: Sea Wisp Louisiana Iris (Wisteria Blue Parent of Jacaranda Lad)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and suits pond margins, rain gardens, or any low spot that stays consistently damp.

directions: Sea Wisp was registered in 1983 by Louisiana iris hybridizer Henry Rowlan, bearing wisteria-blue flowers accented by a raised yellow line signal edged in white, carried on stalks to about three feet and blooming in midseason. It became a notable breeding parent, crossed with 'Spanish Ballet' by Australian hybridizer Heather Pryor to produce the jacaranda-blue 'Jacaranda Lad'. Grow it in full sun in soil or shallow water that stays reliably wet, and divide crowded clumps every few years after bloom to maintain vigor.

common_name: Spanish Ballet Louisiana Iris (Cream Iris Veined Greenish Yellow, Parent of Jacaranda Lad)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and suits pond margins, rain gardens, or any low spot that stays consistently damp.

directions: Spanish Ballet was hybridized by John C. Taylor from a cross of 'Dazzling Star' and 'Watch Out', registered in 1991 and introduced the following year, bearing ruffled cream flowers veined in greenish yellow on 36-inch stalks blooming in midseason. It was later used by Heather Pryor, crossed with 'Sea Wisp', to breed the jacaranda-blue 'Jacaranda Lad'. Grow it in full sun in consistently wet to moist soil, and divide congested clumps every few years after bloom.

common_name: Gaudy Is Good Bearded Iris (Garnet Wine Standards and Red-Spotted Falls)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Gaudy Is Good is grown both for its own bold color and as a line behind modern arilbred breeding.

directions: Gaudy Is Good is a tall bearded iris hybridized by Paul Black, registered in 2007 and introduced in 2010. Garnet-wine standards rise over falls marked with large dark red spots that blend into a lavender-rose band edged in medium brown-garnet, set off by dark gold beards and a slight spicy fragrance. It received an Honorable Mention in 2012, and a sibling seedling from the same cross was later paired with 'Silent Sentry' to breed the arilbred 'Galaxina'. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, keeping rhizome tops exposed in full sun.

common_name: Silent Sentry Arilbred Iris (Honey Yellow and Violet Award of Merit Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in gritty, sharply drained soil, since arilbred irises are especially prone to rot in heavy or wet ground.

directions: Silent Sentry was hybridized by Richard Tasco and registered in 2008 from a cross of 'Energizer' and 'Onlooker'. Light methyl-violet standards with fine veining and an amber midrib rise above gold style arms with lemon-yellow centers and honey-yellow falls marked by veining and a large oval dark burgundy signal, with bright yellow beards, on stalks to about 32 inches blooming midseason to late. It earned an Honorable Mention in 2010 and an Award of Merit in 2012, and has since been used as a parent of several modern arilbreds, including Paul Black's 'Galaxina'. Set rhizomes shallowly with the top surface exposed in gritty, sharply drained soil, and divide congested clumps every two to three years after bloom.

common_name: Tarawera Flow Louisiana Iris (Deep Purple Iris with Gold Signals)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and suits pond margins, rain gardens, or any low spot that stays consistently damp.

directions: Tarawera Flow was registered by New Zealand hybridizer Peter Jackson in 2015 from a cross of 'Garnet Storm Dancer' and 'Far and Away', opening deep velvety purple standards and falls softened by paler purple style arms with darker tips, each petal marked by a recurved gold signal with a raised center line. It blooms late on stalks to about 41 inches and has become a popular modern breeding parent, standing behind cultivars including 'Crowned Royal' and Jackson's own 'Oriental Flight'. Grow it in full sun in heavy, fertile soil kept consistently wet, and divide the expanding rhizome clump every few years to sustain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Little Ruby Slippers Louisiana Iris (Ruby Red Iris Edged in Lemon)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and suits pond margins, rain gardens, or any low spot that stays consistently damp.

directions: Little Ruby Slippers was registered by Bernard Pryor in 2000, bearing heavily ruffled ruby-red petals edged in lemon, with a bright yellow starburst signal and a tall yellow steeple signal rising from a green base on the falls, and ruby-red style arms fringed in lemon over a yellow base. It blooms early to midseason on stalks to about 32 inches and has been used as a breeding parent, crossed with 'Bound for Glory' to produce 'Coral Island'. Grow it in full sun in rich, evenly wet soil typical of Louisiana iris culture, and divide congested clumps every few years after bloom.

common_name: Mac's Blue Heaven Louisiana Iris (Full Violet Self with White Signal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and suits pond margins, rain gardens, or any low spot that stays consistently damp.

directions: Mac's Blue Heaven was registered in 1970 by Louisiana iris and daylily hybridizer W. B. MacMillan and introduced in 1973, bearing a full violet self with a white signal on stalks to about 30 inches, blooming midseason. It is not the most vigorous grower among Louisiana iris, but it has remained in cultivation for its clean color and was later used by Joseph Musacchia, crossed with 'In the Navy', to breed the modern cultivar 'Mama Janice'. Grow it in full sun in rich, consistently wet to moist soil, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain bloom.

common_name: In the Navy Louisiana Iris (Navy Blue Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and suits pond margins, rain gardens, or any low spot that stays consistently damp.

directions: In the Navy was registered by Kevin Vaughn in 2009 from a cross of 'Sea Knight' and 'Beale Street', bearing heavily ruffled navy-blue standards, style arms, and falls, each marked by darker texture veins, a gold signal, and a near-black outline on the falls. It grows tall, reaching 40 to 47 inches, with an unusually long bloom season running from early into late. Joseph Musacchia later crossed it with 'Mac's Blue Heaven' to breed the modern cultivar 'Mama Janice'. Grow it in full sun in rich, consistently wet to moist soil, dividing congested clumps every few years to sustain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Tchoupitoulas Louisiana Iris (Purple Lavender Iris with Red-Violet Streaks)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and suits pond margins, rain gardens, or any low spot that stays consistently damp.

directions: Tchoupitoulas was registered by New Orleans hybridizer Patrick O'Connor in 2002 from a cross of 'Ice Magic' and 'River Road', taking its name from the historic Tchoupitoulas Street along the Mississippi River in New Orleans. Flat purple-lavender standards carry small red-violet lance-shaped streaks near the base, matched by purple-lavender style arms washed in red-violet and falls carrying a red-violet signal area, blooming in late midseason on 36-inch stalks. It was later used by Joseph Musacchia, crossed with 'Queen Jeanne', to breed the award-winning 'Acadian Sky'. Grow it in full sun with rich, constantly wet to moist soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.

common_name: Queen Jeanne Louisiana Iris (Deep Blue Iris with Golden Steeple Signal)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and suits pond margins, rain gardens, or any low spot that stays consistently damp.

directions: Queen Jeanne was hybridized by Heather Pryor and registered in 2003, bearing deep blue, ruffled flowers finely rimmed in lilac, with a clear yellow blotch overlaid by a golden steeple signal on the falls and white style arms blushed violet. It blooms in late midseason on stalks to about 41 inches and was later used by Joseph Musacchia, crossed with 'Tchoupitoulas', to breed the award-winning Louisiana iris 'Acadian Sky'. Grow it in full sun with rich, constantly wet soil typical of Louisiana iris culture, and divide congested clumps every few years after bloom.

common_name: Go Around Bearded Iris (White Plicata Stitched in Pale Blue)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Go Around is grown both as a garden plicata and as a parent behind later Wister Medal breeding.

directions: Go Around was hybridized by Mary Dunn and registered in 1982 from a cross of 'Odyssey' and 'Smoke Rings', bearing wide white flowers finely stitched in pale blue around every ruffled petal edge, with a pale yellow beard, on stalks to about 38 inches blooming midseason. It earned an Honorable Mention in 1985 and was later used by Ron Mullin, crossed with 'Laced Cotton', to breed the John C. Wister Medal-winning 'Rhonda Fleming'. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, keeping rhizome tops exposed in full sun with sharp drainage.

common_name: Laced Cotton Bearded Iris (Ruffled White Historic Schreiner Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Laced Cotton now holds Historic Iris status and is grown both for its own ruffled white flowers and as a parent behind later award winners.

directions: Laced Cotton was bred by Schreiner's Iris Gardens, registered in 1978 and introduced in 1980, producing pure white flowers with extensive lace and ruffling on every petal and lemon-to-near-white beards, on 34-inch stalks blooming midseason to late. A faint green cast tints the petals as the bloom first opens before fading to clean white. It earned an Honorable Mention in 1982 and an Award of Merit in 1984, and Ron Mullin later crossed it with 'Go Around' to breed the Wister Medal-winning 'Rhonda Fleming'. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, keeping rhizomes shallow in full sun.

common_name: Gallant Rogue Bearded Iris (Pink-Lilac Standards and Reddish Purple-Black Falls)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost; Gallant Rogue is grown both for its own fragrant bicolor flowers and as a parent behind later award-winning plicatas.

directions: Gallant Rogue was hybridized by Barry Blyth from a cross of 'Tomorrow's Child' and 'Magic Man', registered in 1989 and introduced in 1990. Pinkish lilac standards flushed rosier along the midrib rise above reddish-purple-to-black falls rimmed in aconite violet, with a small crescent of white lines framing a flame-colored beard and a slight sweet fragrance, on stalks to about 37 inches blooming in late midseason. After Honorable Mention and Favorite Guest Iris honors in 1994, it earned an Award of Merit in 1996, and Keith Keppel later crossed it with 'Witches' Sabbath' to breed 'Local Color'. Divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom, keeping rhizome tops exposed in full sun with sharp drainage.
